strengths: Addresses a practically important and underexplored problem in offline RL: the need for per-dataset hyperparameter tuning of policy-constraint scale, which is costly/infeasible in many real applications.

Proposes a reasonably novel bi-level/meta-learning (MAML-style, second-order differentiable) mechanism to adaptively scale the RL/BC trade-off coefficient during training, going beyond prior 'fixed but locally reweighted' adaptive constraint methods.

Extensive empirical evaluation across 39 datasets spanning four D4RL domains (MuJoCo, Maze2d, AntMaze, Adroit), with a single fixed hyperparameter configuration outperforming several methods that require per-dataset tuning on average.

Includes theoretical analysis (Lipschitz-based bounds, performance-difference lemma application) attempting to justify why the proposed loss terms should guarantee non-negative single-step improvement, plus a longer-horizon performance-gap bound.

Good supporting analyses: learning curves of alpha showing sensible dataset/task-adaptive behavior, runtime overhead analysis showing the method is cheap when kα is tuned, and ablations isolating the effect of the robust critic architecture and each loss component (L1, L2, L3).
Reasonably thorough reproducibility details (hyperparameter tables, hardware/software specs) in the appendix.
weaknesses: There is an unresolved gap between theory and practice: Theorem 4.5's derivation requires a constant w (≈30κ²) multiplying L3 for the guarantee to hold, but the practical algorithm simply sets w=1 'for simplicity,' which the authors themselves flag in Remark 4.1 without rigorously justifying why the guarantee still approximately holds in this regime. This weakens the claimed theoretical performance guarantee as a rigorous certificate for the actual method used.

ASPC's advantage is not consistent across all domains: ReBRAC (with per-dataset tuning) beats ASPC on AntMaze and Adroit, and even wPC (fixed hyperparameters) is competitive/better than ASPC on AntMaze, which somewhat undercuts the framing that a single ASPC configuration uniformly matches or exceeds carefully tuned SOTA baselines; the paper leans on the aggregate 'Total Avg' metric to make this claim, which can mask domain-level shortfalls.

Missing comparisons to some other relevant modern offline RL baselines beyond runtime (e.g., CQL is only shown in the runtime plot, not in the main performance table); no comparison with diffusion-policy-based or transformer-based offline RL methods that are increasingly used as strong baselines.

The three-term outer loss (L1, L2, L3) has a somewhat ad hoc construction motivated by loose asymptotic Taylor-expansion arguments (assuming ΔL_BC/c²_∞ ≪ 1); it is unclear how tight/valid these approximations are in the medium-to-late training regimes actually explored, and no empirical validation of the approximation quality is provided.

Only 4 random seeds are used, which may be insufficient given the very high variance observed in several AntMaze/Adroit results (e.g., large standard deviations in Table 1), making some domain-level comparisons less statistically convincing.

The performance gains partially depend on the 'robust critic' (deeper network + LayerNorm) borrowed from prior work (ReBRAC-style architecture) rather than purely from the proposed adaptive-scaling mechanism; while the ablation attempts to disentangle this, the core algorithmic contribution's standalone marginal benefit could be presented more clearly and quantitatively.

Limited discussion of computational/implementation complexity and stability of the second-order (bilevel) optimization beyond runtime, e.g., sensitivity to the TorchOpt implementation, potential for training instability in more complex environments, or failure cases beyond the reported ablations.

The evaluation remains confined to the standard D4RL benchmark; the authors acknowledge but do not address generalizability to real-world or noisier datasets, limiting evidence for broader significance claimed in the introduction.

strengths: Addresses a practically important and well-motivated problem: the sensitivity of offline RL policy-constraint methods to per-dataset hyperparameter tuning.
Extensive empirical evaluation across 39 datasets spanning four D4RL domains (MuJoCo, Maze2d, AntMaze, Adroit), which is a relatively comprehensive test bed.

Clear ablations isolating the contribution of the robust critic architecture and the individual outer-loss terms (L1, L2, L3), as well as a controlled comparison (Naive/Converged/Linear/Dynamic alpha) that helps justify that dynamic adaptation, not just a better fixed constant, drives the gains.
Runtime analysis shows the second-order meta-learning overhead can be controlled via the update interval kα, making the method practically efficient relative to TD3+BC.

Visualizations of alpha trajectories across dataset quality and tasks provide intuitive, interpretable evidence that the mechanism behaves as intended (favoring BC on high-quality data, RL on low-quality data).
weaknesses: The central theoretical contribution is undermined by its own derivation: Theorem 4.5's guarantee requires L3 to be scaled by a specific constant w = 30κ² derived via Taylor expansion, but the paper explicitly sets w = 1 'for simplicity' (Remark 4.1) without empirical or theoretical justification that this still satisfies the theorem's conditions in practice, making the advertised 'performance improvement guarantee' largely decorative rather than something the implemented algorithm actually satisfies.

The theory relies on multiple unknown/unverified Lipschitz and sup-norm constants (L_Q, L_P, C, c_infinity) that are never estimated or validated empirically, so the bounds in Propositions 4.3/4.4 and Theorems 4.5/4.6 provide limited actionable or falsifiable insight.

The experimental comparison is incomplete relative to the paper's own related-work section: several adaptive policy-constraint methods explicitly discussed (OAP, PRDC, GORL, IEPC, AW) are omitted from the main benchmark table (Table 1), leaving only wPC and A2PR as adaptive baselines; this weakens the claim of outperforming 'other adaptive constraint methods' broadly.

Despite the headline claim of beating meticulously tuned SOTA methods, ASPC actually underperforms the per-dataset-tuned ReBRAC on two of the four domains (AntMaze: 74.5 vs 76.8; Adroit: 55.7 vs 58.6), so the 'wins on average' narrative is driven largely by MuJoCo/Maze2d gains and somewhat overstates uniform superiority.

The method is demonstrated only on a single backbone (TD3+BC); no results are shown integrating ASPC into other backbones (e.g., IQL, CQL, ReBRAC) despite the abstract/future-work framing suggesting broader applicability, limiting evidence of generality.

Several 'meta' hyperparameters (EMA smoothing factor, alpha learning rate/decay, kα, kπ) are fixed and not ablated for sensitivity across tasks, so the claim of a single, tuning-free hyperparameter configuration is only partially substantiated — the method still has multiple knobs whose robustness is unverified.

Only 4 random seeds are used and no statistical significance testing is reported, which is a modest evaluation standard given the many close-margin comparisons (e.g., AntMaze and Adroit domains) in Table 1.

The core technical idea is architecturally heavy (second-order bilevel optimization, three-term outer loss, EMA, detach-based gradient stopping) for what is ultimately tuning a single scalar trade-off coefficient, raising questions about complexity-to-benefit ratio compared to simpler adaptive schemes.

strengths: Addresses a genuinely important and practical problem in offline RL: the need for per-dataset hyperparameter tuning of policy-constraint strength, which is costly and often infeasible in real applications.
Extensive empirical evaluation across 39 datasets spanning four D4RL domains (MuJoCo, Maze2d, AntMaze, Adroit), which is a broader sweep than many comparable papers in this subfield.

The proposed bilevel/second-order differentiable scheme for adapting the RL-BC balance coefficient α is a reasonably novel application of meta-learning-style optimization to this specific problem, and the qualitative behavior of α (increasing for lower-quality data, task-dependent asymptotes) is intuitive and well illustrated (Figs. 3-4, Appendix C).

Reasonably thorough ablations: robust critic architecture, decomposition of the outer loss into L1/L2/L3 components, and a controlled comparison (Naive/Converged/Linear/Dynamic α) that isolates the benefit of dynamic adaptation from simply finding a better fixed α (Table 2) -- this is a nice experimental design choice that strengthens the causal claim.
Runtime analysis shows the method adds only modest overhead over TD3+BC and can be further reduced by increasing the α-update interval, addressing a natural concern about second-order gradients.

A theoretical analysis (Propositions 4.3-4.4, Theorems 4.5-4.6) is provided to motivate the loss design, and the paper is honest about the simplifying assumption needed for Theorem 4.5 and about setting w=1 rather than the theoretically prescribed value (Remark 4.1).
weaknesses: Theoretical guarantees rely on several idealizing assumptions (global Lipschitz continuity of Q and transition kernel, deterministic policies, the condition ΔL_BC∞/c²∞ ≪ 1 for Theorem 4.5) that are not empirically verified on the actual datasets, and the constants (C, L_P, L_Q, κ) in the bounds are never estimated, so the practical predictive power of the theory is limited to qualitative intuition rather than quantitative guarantees.

The gap between theory and implementation is non-trivial: Theorem 4.5's proof suggests L3 should be scaled by a constant w derived from a Taylor expansion, but the paper simply sets w=1 without empirical justification beyond 'achieves competitive results,' weakening the claimed tightness of the theory-practice connection.

Despite the headline claim of outperforming methods with per-dataset tuning, ASPC is not best in AntMaze or Adroit domains (underperforming ReBRAC and/or wPC there), and the paper's framing emphasizes 'Total Avg' superiority while downplaying domain-level shortfalls; some AntMaze results (e.g., Medium-Diverse, Large-Play/Diverse) show visible regressions relative to tuned baselines.

All experiments use the TD3+BC backbone only; despite claiming ASPC is a general framework for balancing RL and BC objectives, there is no empirical demonstration that the approach transfers to other backbones (e.g., CQL, IQL, BCQ), leaving the generality claim largely untested.

Some reported baseline numbers show very large variance (e.g., TD3+BC on hopper-medium-replay: 47.4 ± 35.4), which raises questions about the stability/reliability of the reproduced baselines and could affect the fairness of comparisons.

The bilevel optimization introduces additional hyperparameters (inner/outer learning rates, kπ, kα, EMA smoothing factor) that, while fixed across all 39 datasets in the reported experiments, are not thoroughly analyzed for sensitivity; it is unclear how robust the method would be if these meta-hyperparameters were perturbed, which is somewhat in tension with the paper's single-hyperparameter-configuration narrative.

The paper does not include comparisons against more recent or diverse offline RL baselines beyond CQL/IQL/ReBRAC/wPC/A2PR (e.g., diffusion-based or newer in-sample methods), and does not test on larger/more realistic benchmarks beyond D4RL, which is explicitly deferred to future work.

strengths: Extremely thorough empirical evaluation: 39 D4RL datasets across 4 domains, plus additional OGBench experiments, with multiple ablations (robust critic, loss components, L3 formulation variants, α initialization and learning-rate sensitivity).
Demonstrates broad applicability by integrating the ASPC idea into IQL, CQL, Diffusion-QL, and FQL, showing the bilevel constraint-scaling idea is not specific to TD3+BC.

Provides theoretical analysis (mutual-constraint proposition, single-step and long-horizon performance bounds) that at least qualitatively motivates the design of the outer loss terms L2/L3, and the paper is transparent about assumptions and proofs in the appendix.
Reports runtime overhead analysis showing the second-order updates can be made cheap via a longer α-update interval without much performance loss, addressing a natural practicality concern.
Good qualitative analysis of α dynamics (task- and dataset-quality dependent behavior) that supports the intuitive story of the method and adds interpretability.
weaknesses: The headline claim that ASPC with a single hyperparameter configuration 'outperforms' meticulously tuned SOTA (e.g., ReBRAC) is only true on some aggregated averages; per-domain/per-dataset inspection (Table 1) shows ReBRAC clearly wins on most HalfCheetah tasks and several Adroit tasks, and the 'Total Avg' metric is heavily influenced by Maze2d, whose raw score scale (up to 200+) is much larger than other domains, potentially skewing the unweighted overall comparison.

The theoretical results, while formally proven, rely on strong/idealized assumptions (global Lipschitz continuity of Q and the transition kernel, an 'idealized' update satisfying ΔQ ≥ Φ) that are unlikely to strictly hold for deep neural Q-functions; the practical L3 term is obtained via a first-order Taylor approximation and an ad-hoc rescaling (setting w=1), which weakens the rigor implied by the 'theoretical performance guarantee' framing in the abstract.

Despite the 'single hyperparameter configuration' selling point, the method still contains several sensitive hyperparameters (α initialization, α learning rate, update interval kα) whose sensitivity analysis (Figures 11-12) shows substantial performance swings across domains, suggesting some hidden per-domain tuning was likely needed to select the reported defaults.

The generalization results to other backbones (Table 3, Table 4) are mixed rather than uniformly positive — several individual datasets show performance degradation when ASPC is added (e.g., IQL on halfcheetah-medium and hopper-medium, several OGBench antmaze-giant tasks with FQL+ASPC declining by double digits), which is somewhat at odds with the paper's claim of 'consistent' improvement.

The set of 'adaptive policy constraint' baselines is limited to wPC and A2PR; other recent adaptive/auxiliary-model approaches mentioned in related work (PRDC, GORL, IEPC, OAP) are not empirically compared, leaving the competitive landscape for the core claimed contribution incompletely tested.

Ablations and dynamics analyses are largely presented as domain-averaged bar/line charts, which can mask important per-task variance and failure cases (e.g., the poor AntMaze/Adroit performance is explained post hoc via a sparse-reward argument and partially patched with an additional advantage-weighting trick in the appendix, suggesting the core method alone is not fully sufficient in this setting).

strengths: Addresses a practically important problem: the sensitivity of policy-constraint offline RL methods to the scale hyperparameter across datasets of varying quality.

Very extensive empirical evaluation spanning 39 D4RL datasets across four domains, plus additional experiments on OGBench and integration with four other offline RL backbones (IQL, CQL, Diffusion-QL, FQL).
Thorough set of ablations (robust critic, loss-term decomposition, formulation variants of L3, sensitivity to initial alpha and learning rate) that probe the method's internal workings.
The qualitative analysis of alpha trajectories (Figures 3-4) provides an intuitive and reasonably convincing illustration of adaptive behavior across dataset quality and task type.
Runtime analysis shows the second-order procedure can be made cheap via infrequent outer updates.
weaknesses: The theoretical contribution is largely decorative rather than functional: Theorem 4.4 ('if ΔQ ≥ Φ then performance is non-decreasing') is close to a tautology and provides no real guarantee that the actual learned update satisfies this condition in practice. The derivation of L3 (Appendix A.3) relies on a truncated second-order Taylor expansion plus an arbitrary rescaling ('we set w to 1' and substitute (ΔQ)^2 for an unrelated Lipschitz-constant-based coefficient) that is not rigorously justified, giving a false sense of formal rigor to what is essentially a heuristic loss term.

The headline claim of a 35%/36.6% average improvement is driven overwhelmingly by the Maze2d domain, where variances are extremely large (e.g., ASPC umaze 128.1±31.8, large 195.8±31.3) and overlap substantially with baselines; on AntMaze and Adroit ASPC is actually outperformed by ReBRAC despite the latter requiring per-dataset tuning, undermining the paper's central claim that a single configuration can match/exceed tuned baselines across the board.

The generality experiments (Section 5.6, Table 3) show inconsistent results when ASPC is grafted onto IQL/CQL/Diffusion-QL, with several individual datasets showing performance degradation; the paper's own conclusion admits these gains are much smaller than for TD3+BC, weakening the 'broad generality' claim made in the abstract.

Experimental fairness is questionable: the 'robust critic' (3-layer + LayerNorm) architecture is explicitly added to TD3+BC and wPC baselines but it is unclear whether the same architectural upgrade was consistently and equivalently applied to A2PR and the other integrated baselines (CQL, IQL, Diffusion-QL, FQL), making cross-method comparisons less controlled than claimed.

Many reported standard deviations (particularly for AntMaze, Adroit, and OGBench) are large enough that the differences between ASPC and the strongest baselines are not clearly significant, yet the paper repeatedly asserts SOTA/best performance without statistical testing across only 4 seeds.

The added complexity (second-order bilevel optimization, extra hyperparameters such as kα, ηα, EMA factor, initial α) partially contradicts the paper's main selling point of eliminating per-dataset tuning burden, since several of these meta-hyperparameters still require non-trivial selection and sensitivity analysis (Appendix F) shows performance is fairly sensitive to them.

Novelty is incremental: applying MAML-style bilevel/second-order optimization to a scalar trade-off coefficient is a fairly direct application of existing bilevel optimization machinery (Finn et al. 2017; Franceschi et al. 2018) to a known problem (policy-constraint scale selection) already targeted by closely related prior work (wPC, A2PR, GORL).

strengths: Extremely thorough empirical evaluation: 39 D4RL datasets across 4 domains plus 10 OGBench tasks, with multiple seeds and strong baselines (TD3+BC, IQL, wPC, A2PR, ReBRAC).
Addresses a practically important and underexplored problem: eliminating per-dataset hyperparameter tuning for the RL-BC trade-off in policy-constraint offline RL.

Rich set of ablations (robust critic necessity, individual loss term contributions L1/L2/L3, alternative L3 formulations, kα update interval vs runtime/performance, initial α and learning rate sensitivity) that help isolate the source of gains.

Demonstrates generality by integrating the adaptive-scaling idea into IQL, CQL, Diffusion-QL, and FQL, and testing on a goal-conditioned benchmark (OGBench), showing the idea is not narrowly tied to TD3+BC.
Reasonable qualitative analysis of α dynamics (dataset-quality adaptivity, task adaptivity, training-phase adaptivity) that is intuitive and consistent with the algorithm's design.
Runtime analysis shows the second-order update overhead can be amortized with infrequent α updates, making the method practical.
Code, hyperparameters, and reproducibility details are provided in detail.
weaknesses: The theoretical results are more illustrative than rigorous: Theorem 4.4 only shows an 'idealized' condition guarantees non-decrease, while the actual loss L3 is derived via a second-order Taylor expansion under an unverified small-ratio assumption (ΔL_BC∞/c∞² ≪ 1) and then further rescaled by an ad hoc weight w=1 'in practice,' so the link between the stated guarantee and the deployed algorithm is heuristic rather than proven.

Gains attributed to 'adaptive scaling' are partly confounded with the architectural change (3-layer critic + LayerNorm, the 'robust critic'); the ablation shows ASPC fails without RC, suggesting the core adaptive mechanism depends heavily on an orthogonal architectural fix rather than being self-contained.

Despite the headline claim of beating per-dataset-tuned SOTA, ReBRAC (dataset-specific tuning) still wins on many individual tasks and on the AntMaze domain average (76.8 vs 74.5), and dominates several MuJoCo subsets (e.g., HalfCheetah), so the 'outperforms SOTA' framing is only true in aggregate, not uniformly.

On OGBench, ASPC occasionally underperforms simpler baselines with large variance (e.g., antmaze-giant-task3: 18±13 vs ReBRAC 34±22), and some FQL+ASPC results show clear degradations (e.g., task4 ↓12.5%, task1 ↓50%), slightly undercutting the 'consistent gains' claim in Section 5.6/5.7.

The bilevel/MAML-style approach to hyperparameter adaptation is methodologically incremental relative to existing bilevel optimization and meta-learning literature (Finn et al. 2017; Franceschi et al. 2018); the core novelty is mainly the specific instantiation of inner/outer losses for the α coefficient.

No comparison against generic automatic hyperparameter optimization baselines (e.g., population-based training, simple online schedules beyond the paper's own 'linear α' ablation) that could achieve similar single-configuration robustness without the second-order machinery.
Some ablation explanations (e.g., why L2 alone suffices for MuJoCo/Adroit but not AntMaze) are post-hoc narrative justifications tied loosely to Proposition 4.2 rather than independently validated.
The paper is very dense with many deferred theoretical derivations and appendix-heavy content, which could hinder clarity and independent verification of the proofs within the main text.
